facts.claim: Kurt Cobain's "And I Love Her" is a cover of The Beatles' 1964 song of the same name.
The track appears on Montage of Heck: The Home Recordings, which was released on November 13, 2015. It came as a 31-track deluxe edition or a 13-track standard edition.
The album is the soundtrack to Brett Morgen's Cobain documentary Montage of Heck. Morgen went through Cobain's archives of home recordings and rare tracks to curate it.
Morgen found the raw, acoustic take on a random tape and used it in his film.
The cover first surfaced online in April 2015 but was taken down soon after. It was later made available officially through Spotify.
Last.fm says the recording was likely made in 1987 or 1988 and was released in 2015 as the sole single from the soundtrack. This dating comes from a user-edited wiki.
A 7-inch single pairs "And I Love Her" with an early demo of "Sappy". It was scheduled for November 20, 2015.

Morgen found the source cassettes when Courtney Love and Frances Bean Cobain approached him about a documentary. He chose to release material from cassette number 54, titled Montage of Heck, out of 108 tapes.
Morgen said the home recordings show another side of Cobain, an artistic outlet he couldn't fully use in a three-piece band. He compared the release to Bob Dylan's Bootleg Series.

The film's title comes from a collage Cobain made on a 4-track cassette recorder around 1988. Cobain was born in 1967 to a car mechanic father and a waitress mother, and his daughter Frances Bean Cobain was a co-executive producer on the film.

research.lineage: It is a raw, lo-fi acoustic home-tape cover of a Beatles song from Nirvana frontman Kurt Cobain's private cassette archive, released as a solo companion to the Montage of Heck documentary.

draft:
The only time **"And I Love Her"** speaks to the person it's about is in the middle, in two words: "Hold you near me." Everywhere else she's "her," described to someone else, held at the distance of a report. Then for one line the singer turns and talks to her directly before turning back. Paul McCartney wrote that shift into the Beatles' 1964 original. Kurt Cobain keeps it, and in his hands it lands harder, because nothing in the recording is trying to sound sure of itself.

What's here is one acoustic guitar, strummed slowly, with a relaxed tempo that seems to drag a little behind the beat, and a voice in a low-middle range that sounds raw and a bit strained. There are no harmonies. The Beatles' version had a delicate guitar figure and a light touch of percussion. This has a small, dry room and a person sitting in it. The roughness doesn't fight the song. It changes what the song is about.

The lyric is almost pure plain devotion: "She gives me everything / And tenderly." It's a song with no conflict in it. No rival, no leaving, no doubt, just stars, a dark sky, and a promise that "this love of mine / Will never die." Sung cleanly, that promise sounds like a fact. Sung in a strained voice at a dragging pace, it sounds like something the singer needs to say out loud to keep believing it. The words stay certain while the voice carrying them sounds worn, and the recording never settles which one to trust. The song ends where it always does, on "And I love her," a statement made to nobody in particular.

Cobain wasn't making a record here. Brett Morgen found the take on a random tape while digging through Cobain's archive of home cassettes for his documentary *Montage of Heck*, and used it in the film. It leaked online in April 2015, came down, and then arrived officially as part of *Montage of Heck: The Home Recordings*, with a 7-inch pairing it with an early demo of "Sappy." Morgen described these tapes as another side of Cobain, an outlet he couldn't fully use in a three-piece band, and compared the project to Dylan's Bootleg Series. That fits. This is a songwriter learning a song he loved by playing it alone, and the private setting gives a love song a kind of shyness the original never had.

What stays with you is that single turn to "you." For one line, a person singing alone in a room stops describing love and speaks to the one he loves.
